articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47M stormwater backlog grows as drainage projects stall
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fund, less than a third of promised improvements are complete. Commissioners blame supply costs. Residents blame commissioners.
brief: Only 28% of drainage projects promised in the 2023 stormwater referendum have been completed, leaving $47 million in work unfunded or delayed
Commissioners point to inflation and supply chain disruptions; residents in flood-prone neighborhoods say the county overpromised and underdelivered
Annual flooding costs county residents an estimated $12 million in property damage, according to county emergency management data
articles.body:
The culvert under Fairfield Drive in Brownsville has been on Escambia County's priority list for six years. Every summer, the same thing happens. Rain pools at the low point where the road dips. Water backs into yards. Septic systems overflow. Residents call the county. The county adds it to the list.

"They came out here in 2021 with clipboards," said Darlene Washington, who has lived on Fairfield Drive for 31 years. "They measured everything. Took pictures. Told us we were definitely on the schedule."

She's still waiting.

Washington's neighborhood is one of 64 drainage improvement zones identified in the county's 2022 stormwater master plan—the document that formed the backbone of a successful 2023 referendum asking voters to dedicate a portion of gas tax revenue to fixing chronic flooding problems. The measure passed with 58% support after commissioners promised a systematic approach to a problem that had festered for decades.

Three years later, less than a third of that work is done.

The numbers

According to county infrastructure records obtained through a public records request, Escambia County has completed 18 of the 64 drainage projects outlined in the master plan. Another 12 are under construction. The remaining 34 are either in design phase, awaiting permits, or—in the case of 11 projects—haven't moved past the planning stage at all.

The original cost estimate for the full 64-project list was $62 million spread over five years. The current estimate sits at $109 million. That leaves a $47 million gap between what the dedicated fund can cover and what the work actually costs.

County Administrator Wes Moreno called the situation "challenging but manageable" during a June budget workshop.

"We're dealing with a construction environment that nobody predicted," Moreno told commissioners. "Concrete costs are up 40% from 2022. Pipe prices have doubled in some cases. The same projects simply cost more than they did when voters approved the plan."

He's not wrong about the numbers. Federal construction cost indices show infrastructure materials rose 23% between 2022 and 2025, with drainage-specific components climbing even higher due to demand from federal infrastructure spending nationwide.

But critics say the county's problems run deeper than inflation.

Design delays and contractor disputes

Of the 34 incomplete projects, 19 have experienced what county documents categorize as "administrative delays"—a term covering everything from permit complications to engineering redesigns to disputes with contractors.

The Myrtle Grove drainage basin project, budgeted at $4.2 million, has been redesigned three times since 2024 after initial plans failed to account for wetland setback requirements. The project is now 14 months behind schedule and $800,000 over its original budget.

The West Pensacola trunk line replacement, meant to reduce flooding along Mobile Highway, sat dormant for seven months in 2025 while the county and its primary contractor disputed change order costs. The contractor eventually walked off the job. The county rebid the work at a 35% higher price.

Commissioner Steven Barry, whose District 5 includes several delayed projects, said the problems reflect broader dysfunction in county project management.

"We've got good engineers," Barry said in an interview. "What we don't have is enough of them, and we don't have enough oversight on the contracting side. Projects slip because nobody's watching the timeline."

Barry has proposed hiring a dedicated stormwater program manager—a position that exists in most Florida counties of similar size. The proposal has stalled twice in budget discussions.

Flood costs mount

While the county debates management structure, residents keep getting wet.

Escambia County Emergency Management estimates that flooding causes roughly $12 million in annual property damage across unincorporated areas—a figure that doesn't include damage within Pensacola city limits or indirect costs like lost wages and temporary housing.

The Brownsville and Brentwood neighborhoods, both predominantly Black communities that rank among the county's lowest-income census tracts, experience flooding at rates three times higher than the county average, according to 911 call data analyzed by The Flightline.

These are the same neighborhoods where projects have seen the longest delays.

"You start to wonder if it's a coincidence," said Marcus Williams, president of the Brownsville Neighborhood Association. "They fixed the drainage over by Cordova Mall pretty quick. That shopping center floods, and suddenly there's money. Our streets flood, and we're still on a list."

County officials reject any suggestion that project prioritization reflects bias.

"Projects are ranked by engineering criteria—flood frequency, property damage potential, public safety impact," said county spokeswoman Amber Tyner. "Those rankings were established in the master plan before any specific projects were funded."

But the master plan itself ranked the Brownsville culvert as a "high priority" project in 2022. It remains unscheduled.

What happens next

The commission faces a decision this fall. The dedicated stormwater fund generates approximately $8 million annually. At current cost projections, that funding level would take more than 13 years to complete the remaining work—assuming no additional cost increases.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh has floated the idea of returning to voters with a request for additional funding, either through a property tax increase or a bond measure.

"We made promises," Bergosh said during the June workshop. "If we can't keep them with current revenue, we need to be honest about that and give voters a choice."

That honesty might be politically expensive. The 2023 referendum passed partly because commissioners assured voters the gas tax dedication would be sufficient. Going back for more money three years later, with two-thirds of the work undone, invites obvious questions about planning and competence.

For Darlene Washington, the political calculations matter less than the water in her yard.

"Every time it rains hard, I move my furniture," she said. "I've got sandbags in my garage ready to go. That's my flood plan now. Because clearly the county doesn't have one."

The commission's next budget workshop is scheduled for August 18. Stormwater funding is on the agenda.

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: The last fish house on Joe Patti's block
articles.dek: A seafood district that once stretched six blocks is down to a handful of holdouts. What happens when the cold storage goes condo.
brief: Pensacola's historic seafood district has shrunk from six blocks to scattered holdouts over three decades
Gulf Ice & Cold Storage, the last commercial fish house adjacent to Joe Patti's, faces pressure from a proposed mixed-use development
City planners and preservationists debate whether working waterfront protections can survive market forces
articles.body:
The smell hits you first. Brine and diesel and something older—the mineral funk of fish blood soaked into concrete that no amount of bleaching will ever lift. At 5:47 a.m. on a Thursday, Tommy Nguyen backs his box truck to the loading dock at Gulf Ice & Cold Storage and cuts the engine. He's been making this run for eleven years. He doesn't know how many more he has left.

"Used to be you couldn't get a spot on this block before six," Nguyen said, gesturing at the empty lot next door where Bayou Seafood Processing stood until 2019. "Now I'm the only one here half the time."

Gulf Ice sits at the corner of A Street and Main, one block east of Joe Patti's Seafood, the landmark fish market that draws tourists by the busload and locals who remember when you could buy shrimp straight off the boat. The cold storage facility is the last commercial fish house on a block that once held five. Soon it may hold none.

A district in retreat

Pensacola's seafood district stretched from Cervantes Street to the commercial docks in the 1970s, a working waterfront that processed millions of pounds of Gulf catch annually. Shrimp boats unloaded at dawn. Ice houses ran three shifts. The air tasted like salt.

Today the footprint has collapsed. A 2024 inventory by the Pensacola Downtown Improvement Board counted four active seafood processing facilities within the original district boundaries, down from twenty-three in 1985. The rest became parking lots, storage units, and in two cases, condominium developments marketed to retirees seeking "authentic waterfront living."

Joe Patti's survives as retail, not processing—a destination rather than a node in a supply chain. The boats that once fed it now motor to Panama City or Bayou La Batre, where the infrastructure still exists to handle volume.

"We're not a port anymore," said Carmen Delgado, a fish house supervisor who started at Gulf Ice in 1998. "We're a backdrop."

The Cervantes Street proposal

In March, a Tampa-based development group called Bayshore Partners LLC submitted preliminary plans to the city for a mixed-use project on the 2.3-acre parcel that includes Gulf Ice and two adjacent lots. The proposal calls for 186 residential units, 12,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and structured parking. Estimated project cost: $67 million.

The plans describe the ground-floor retail as "marine-adjacent commercial" without specifying what that means. Renderings show a kayak rental shop and a restaurant with outdoor seating facing the water.

Gulf Ice operates on a month-to-month lease. Owner Frank Corso, whose family has run the facility since 1962, said he was notified of the development interest in January but has not received a formal termination notice.

"They're not required to tell me anything until thirty days out," Corso said. "Sixty years my family's been here. I could find out by certified mail."

Bayshore Partners did not respond to multiple interview requests. Property records show the company purchased the parcels in August 2025 for $4.2 million.

What protection looks like

Pensacola has no working waterfront ordinance. Unlike Apalachicola, which requires a percentage of harbor-adjacent parcels to maintain commercial fishing uses, or Tarpon Springs, which restricts certain dock conversions, Pensacola's zoning code treats seafood processing the same as any light industrial use: legal where permitted, but with no special status.

City Council member Jared Wilson, whose District 6 includes the seafood district, introduced a resolution in May calling for a "working waterfront study." The resolution passed 6-1, directing planning staff to inventory remaining maritime commercial uses and evaluate preservation tools. A report is due in September.

"We keep saying we want to keep our character," Wilson said in an interview. "But character doesn't preserve itself. It requires choices."

Critics of waterfront protections argue they amount to economic interference. At the May council meeting, Pensacola Chamber of Commerce representative Diane Hurst testified that "restricting property rights to preserve a nostalgic vision of the waterfront" would discourage investment.

The lone dissenting vote on the study resolution came from Council member Bill Garrett, who called the effort "a solution looking for a problem."

"The market is telling us what these properties are worth," Garrett said. "We shouldn't pretend we know better."

The math of fish

Corso provided financial documents showing Gulf Ice processed 1.8 million pounds of seafood in 2025, generating $340,000 in gross revenue. His operating margin, he said, runs about 6 percent after labor, utilities, and maintenance on equipment that requires constant repair.

The property's assessed value, according to Escambia County records, is $1.1 million. Based on the Bayshore purchase price, the land alone is now worth roughly $1.8 million per acre.

"I can make fish work or I can sell the lease and retire," Corso said. "My kids don't want this. Nobody's kids want this."

Nguyen, the truck driver, sources shrimp and snapper from Gulf Ice for three restaurants in the Pensacola metro area. If the facility closes, his next-nearest option is 47 miles away in Bon Secour, Alabama. The added fuel and time would cost him, he estimates, $180 per trip.

"The restaurants won't pay more," Nguyen said. "I just make less."

What remains

At Joe Patti's on a Saturday afternoon, the parking lot overflows. Families pose for photos beneath the vintage sign. Inside, tourists fill coolers with cleaned snapper, unaware or unconcerned that the fish was trucked in from somewhere else.

The market remains Pensacola's most visible connection to its maritime past—a past that grows more curated each year. The seafood is real. The setting is preserved. The working waterfront that once surrounded it is mostly memory.

Three blocks east, past the empty lots and the storage facilities with faded "For Lease" signs, Gulf Ice & Cold Storage runs its last compressor through another summer. The ice machine churns. The loading dock fills and empties. Tommy Nguyen finishes his haul and heads north toward the restaurants that will serve his catch tonight.

The block is quiet by 7 a.m. By noon, it's silent.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola flight training delays ripple into second year
articles.dek: Instructor shortages and aging T-6 trainers have pushed graduation timelines back months. Student naval aviators are waiting longer than any class since 2019.
brief: Student naval aviators at NAS Pensacola now wait an average of 14 months between commissioning and first flight, up from 9 months in 2023
Training Air Wing Five reports 23% of T-6B Texan II aircraft grounded for maintenance at any given time
Navy officials cite instructor pilot retention as the primary bottleneck, with commercial airlines offering triple military pay
articles.body:
The morning brief at Training Squadron Three started forty minutes late on a Tuesday in June. Eight student naval aviators sat in a classroom on the second floor of Building 633, waiting for an instructor who was covering two other flights that day.

When Lieutenant Commander Sarah Okonkwo finally arrived, she apologized and got straight to the lesson. She would apologize again that afternoon, and twice more that week. There aren't enough of her to go around.

"We're asking instructors to do the work of one and a half people," said Captain Marcus Reilly, commanding officer of Training Air Wing Five. "They're performing. But the math doesn't hold forever."

The math hasn't held for more than a year now. Student naval aviators arriving at NAS Pensacola for primary flight training face the longest wait times since 2019, when a shooting at the base disrupted operations for months. The current delays have no single cause and no clear end date.

The numbers

Navy data obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request shows the average time between a student's commissioning and their first training flight has stretched to 14 months. In fiscal year 2023, that figure was 9 months. In 2021, it was 7.

The delays compound at each stage. Students wait longer to start ground school. They wait longer between simulator sessions. They wait longer for aircraft availability. By graduation, a class that should have finished in 12 months has taken 18.

"You have ensigns who've been in Pensacola for almost two years and haven't touched a stick," said one instructor pilot who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to discuss training metrics. "That's not what they signed up for. That's not what the Navy needs."

Training Air Wing Five operates approximately 140 T-6B Texan II turboprop trainers across three squadrons at NAS Pensacola and NAS Whiting Field in Milton. On any given day, about 23% of those aircraft are grounded for maintenance, according to wing officials. The T-6B entered service in 2010. The average airframe has logged more than 6,000 flight hours.

Parts availability has tightened as the aircraft age. A hydraulic actuator that once took two weeks to source now takes six. Contractors report backorders on components that weren't backorders three years ago.

The instructor problem

Aircraft maintenance explains part of the delay. The larger part is people.

The Navy needs instructor pilots to train student pilots. Instructor pilots are experienced aviators who've completed fleet tours and returned to Pensacola for shore duty. The job requires patience, precision and a willingness to spend three years in the right seat while someone else learns.

Fewer pilots are volunteering for it.

"Commercial aviation is hiring everyone they can find," said Captain Reilly. "A lieutenant with 2,000 hours can walk into Delta or United and start at $120,000. We can't match that. We're not trying to match that. We're asking them to serve for other reasons."

The reasons don't always win. Navy retention data shows instructor pilot billets at Training Air Wing Five are filled at 81% of authorized levels, down from 94% in fiscal year 2022. The shortage is worse in specific communities. Helicopter instructor billets are at 74%.

Commander David Tran left the Navy in 2024 after a tour as a T-6 instructor. He now flies for Southwest Airlines out of Houston.

"I loved teaching," Tran said in a phone interview. "I did not love watching my students sit around for months because we couldn't get them in the air. I did not love telling my wife I'd be home at six and walking in at nine because I picked up extra flights. The quality of life calculation changed."

The ripple effect

Delays at NAS Pensacola ripple forward through the entire naval aviation pipeline. Students who finish primary training late arrive late to advanced training at bases in Texas, Mississippi and California. Those pipelines have their own constraints. Delays stack.

The effect reaches the fleet. Carrier air wings and helicopter squadrons receive new pilots later than planned. Deployment schedules tighten. Experienced pilots extend their tours to cover gaps, which burns them out faster, which makes them more likely to leave, which makes the instructor shortage worse.

"It's a feedback loop," said Mackenzie Eaglen, a defense analyst at the American Enterprise Institute who studies military readiness. "You can't train your way out of a training shortage if the trainers keep leaving."

The Navy has tried incentives. Instructor pilots now receive $35,000 annual bonuses, up from $25,000 in 2023. The service has experimented with allowing some instructors to work four-day weeks. It has fast-tracked certain administrative processes to reduce paperwork burden.

So far, the incentives have slowed the bleeding. They haven't stopped it.

Waiting in Pensacola

Ensign James Cortez commissioned from the Naval Academy in May 2025. He arrived at NAS Pensacola in August. As of July 2026, he has not begun primary flight training.

"I run. I work out. I study. I wait," Cortez said, standing outside the Aviation Preflight Indoctrination building on a recent Wednesday. "My roommate from Annapolis is already in Meridian doing jets. I'm still here doing nothing."

Cortez is not doing nothing. He completed ground school in November. He passed his swimming qualifications in December. He has logged 47 hours in the T-6 simulator. But simulators don't count toward the flight hours he needs, and flight hours require aircraft and instructors.

He estimates he's four months from his first flight. His original timeline projected that flight for February 2026.

"You try not to get bitter," he said. "Everyone here is in the same situation. But you see your friends progressing and you're just... here."

The base has expanded recreational and educational offerings for students in holding patterns. The Navy College Program added online course options. The base gym extended hours. The MWR office organized more off-base trips.

None of it substitutes for flying.

What comes next

Captain Reilly said Training Air Wing Five expects to receive 12 additional T-6B aircraft by the end of fiscal year 2027, transferred from a training squadron in Texas that is transitioning to a newer trainer. The additional aircraft should reduce maintenance pressure.

The instructor shortage is harder to solve.

"We need the airlines to stop hiring, or we need to make Navy life more attractive, or both," Reilly said. "I control neither of those things. What I control is making sure the instructors we have feel valued and supported. That's what I focus on."

Lieutenant Commander Okonkwo finished her Tuesday brief at 0847. She had eight minutes before her next student showed up. She used them to answer emails.

"I could complain," she said. "I choose not to. These students need someone to teach them. I'm someone. So I teach."

She logged four flights that day, two more than her scheduled load. She was home by eight.
